As a redditor since 2010 I have seen the site's quality behave inversely as its popularity increased. For me the core of reddit was always the small subreddits that catered to specific, often niche, interests. One of my favorite games is old school runescape. The subreddit for it, r/2007scape, is a great place to see pictures of people playing the game and discuss new and potential content updates. However, it is the only subreddit for the game, and also the only one that game developers read on a daily basis. The subreddit has become very restrictive in terms of what you can post and top posts are often deleted--sometimes more than once. Shadowbanning is rampant. It's depressing to browse /new and constantly see posts with 3 comments, and when you click on them only 2 show up. As a top contributor, I have been shadowbanned from this subreddit multiple times. I never receive an explanation when I request one in modmail which is particularly annoying because I'm probably more familiar with the subreddit rules than most. Eventually I decided to create a subreddit of my own with the idea of only deleting posts that contained dangerous links or hateful language--let the community decide what's good. As soon as I ran this idea through them in modmail I was banned from the subreddit and my subreddit's name flagged as spam in theirs.

Pretty much the first thing I did when I came here today is to see what v/2007scape looks like...and it's being squatted by one of the founding mods from the reddit version. So my question is this: what exactly is going to change if voat becomes popular? Will it just be mods from reddit squatting the same subs they mod on the former? How will you prevent users with history of poor transparency from implementing the same thing here? For the record voat does look more promising than reddit and I'll definitely be browsing v/all.

California governor pitches amnesty on traffic debt for poor

From the title I thought I'd oppose this as it seemed to give the poor freedom from traffic laws. However, after reading I was amazed at how traffic fines have skyrocketed - $490 for running a red light. This is hugely regressive. With so many people living paycheck to paycheck, they simply can't afford to pay (in which case the penalty raised the fine to $800). What's worse is that these fines are a major source of revenue for the court system. If everyone faced a fine of a full week's paycheck for a traffic violation, I think there would be revolt.
If you didn't read the report on the fergeson system, take a look. Worst case scenario on regressive policy and revenue generation.

I think a better discussion would be whether minor traffic violations should be used as a revenue stream. Sure we don't want a few individuals endangering others but having a highway drop from 100 to 50 is dangerous and used solely as a revenue generator for tickets and seizing cars where they can.
